content.title: About
content.content: Dry milk is a dehydrated dairy product obtained by evaporating water from whole milk or its components. It retains most nutrients, stores easily, and reconstitutes quickly with water to produce liquid milk when needed.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Dry milk was used in expeditions and military campaigns because of its long shelf life.
The first commercial process for producing dry milk was developed in the early 20th century in the United States.
It is often added to confectionery, sauces, and infant formulas to improve flavor and nutritional value.
In some countries dry milk is an important calcium source where fresh milk is scarce.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Dry milk provides a high amount of calcium, essential for bone and teeth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: It contains all essential amino acids, making it a complete protein source.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Dry milk retains vitamins B2, B12 and niacin, supporting energy metabolism.

items.title: Convenient storage
items.content: Lack of moisture allows long‑term storage without refrigeration while preserving nutrients.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Dry milk contains lactose, so individuals with intolerance should choose lactose‑free alternatives.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People allergic to casein or whey may experience reactions.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Some dry milks are sweetened; check the label if you need to limit sugar.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: To reconstitute, dissolve 1 part dry milk in 4–5 parts cold water, stirring thoroughly. Add dry milk to dough, sauces, cereals, coffee or tea to enhance flavor and nutrition.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry milk in a sealed container in a cool, dry place away from direct light. After opening, use within 6–12 months for best quality.
